cells.tense: The work you keep at by repetition is lit from the inside now.
cells.ask: Show one person the half-finished piece before it's done — the version that isn't ready — and let showing it hand you back the next step.
cells.core:
You're in a place where the practice has steadied. The hours you put in on the thing you care about are feeding the picture rather than chasing it, and the picture and the plan sit at the same table. When a piece is rough, you work it rather than announce it, and the work itself keeps the direction honest.

What's hard here is quieter than it sounds: the steady time is also solitary time, and it can run long without anyone seeing it. Today's step is to say where the work actually stands, to one person, before it's finished. And notice what that leaves you free to feed: not a polished version for the room, but the momentum of the practice itself, moving toward what you want to build.

cells.tense: You're living in a finished room while today's work is still on the bench.
cells.ask: Pick one unfinished thing on your list, say out loud to one person that it's unfinished, then leave it alone for the rest of today.
cells.core:
On an ordinary good day, you sit down with the piece in front of you and let it be mid-shape. You refine what's there, you don't force it into the version you already pictured, and the practice carries you through the next hour.

Lately the pictured version has moved in ahead. The flat hour with no shape yet sits inside a finished scene, so plain repetition feels secondary — and the practice that needs your hands starts answering to a picture that hasn't happened. What's hard is that the picture protects something: as long as you're inside it, the real day can't disappoint and the real thing can't be measured against it. Naming one piece as unfinished, to somebody who's actually in the room with you, hands the day back to you. And what's wanted here isn't more picturing — it's looking after what's actually growing today, at the pace it's actually going.

cells.tense: You stopped walking into the part of the work that has to be touched before it can be shaped.
cells.ask: Set the one thing you've been circling on the table for ten minutes today — hands on it, no article, no video — and let a plain read of it arrive on its own.
cells.core:
On a steady day, you pick something up and hold it without needing to know yet what it's for. You try a step, you see where it lands, you don't require the label first. The work moves by small, direct recognitions that come without being argued for.

Lately the fog itself has started to read as a place to stay out of. Only what can be named and measured gets touched; the rest of the work drifts past, and the practice thins out with it. What's hard is that staying on the safe, labeled surfaces keeps the door open for anyone to walk through — and it also keeps the work from ever fully arriving. Pushing harder at the same measured edge won't break it. Put the actual thing on the table, no explanation nearby. Ten minutes. Not to finish. To let a small, clear sight of it land, and to trust it long enough to see what it says.

cells.tense: The picture you're building toward is already shaping your days, and the credit is going to circumstance.
cells.ask: Choose one thing in the room and say out loud, to no one, what you want it to become — then say out loud that you chose to picture it that way.
cells.core:
On an ordinary day, you know what you're working toward. You sit down with the piece, you make a small move toward a shape you've picked, and the practice and the destination hold together in your hands. Mid-afternoon, you could say out loud what you're trying to make and why.

Right now that choice has slid out of frame. Days get made and then described as what the week threw at you — demands, then luck — and the aim inside them gets treated as something that arrived on its own. What's hard is that when the practice turns into strain, there's nothing on the table to ask about, because the aim driving it hasn't been claimed. Solitude stays the room where the work gets made; naming one thing you want, in your own voice, before it's finished, changes nothing about the room and everything about whose hands it's in.
cells.sheetLine: You're already aiming at something. You've been calling that circumstance.
